Question: Exactly three of the interior angles of a convex polygon are obtuse. What is the maximum number of sides of such a polygon?
Solution:
Let the polygon have \(n\) sides. Convexity makes each of its three obtuse angles less than \(180^\circ\). Every other interior angle is at most \(90^\circ\). Comparing these bounds with the polygon's interior-angle sum gives
\[
180(n-2)<3\cdot180+90(n-3).
\]
Simplifying,
\[
180n-360<90n+270,
\qquad n<7.
\]
Thus the polygon has at most \(6\) sides. The strict inequality matters because an obtuse angle cannot equal \(180^\circ\).

To show that six sides are possible, start with an equilateral triangle. At each vertex, cut off a small triangular corner using a cut perpendicular to one of the two incident sides. Choose the cuts small enough that the removed corners do not meet. Each removed triangle has angles \(60^\circ,90^\circ,30^\circ\), so its cut creates interior angles of \(90^\circ\) and \(150^\circ\) in the remaining polygon.

The three cuts replace the original three vertices with six vertices and preserve convexity. The resulting hexagon has three right angles and exactly three obtuse angles. Therefore the maximum is \(\boxed{6}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
